discovery: Quantum simulation of many-body physics with ultracold atoms in optical lattices and arrays of individually controlled Rydberg atoms

nominees.name: Immanuel Bloch
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Germany

nominees.name: Antoine Browaeys
nominees.affiliation: Laboratoire Charles Fabry, Institut d'Optique Graduate School, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, France

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum simulation
motivation: Feynman proposed simulating quantum matter with controllable quantum systems. The nominees made this real. Immanuel Bloch observed the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition of atoms in optical lattices and then imaged and controlled strongly correlated matter one atom at a time. Antoine Browaeys and Mikhail Lukin built reconfigurable arrays of individually trapped atoms held in optical tweezers and entangled through Rydberg interactions. On these platforms they studied quantum magnetism, quantum phase transitions and topological spin liquids, and ran some of the first programmable quantum processors. The approach relies on entanglement and on control of single quantum objects, the same ingredients that Bell tests turned from a philosophical question into a laboratory resource. Their work answers deep questions about many-body physics that no classical computer can handle, and it has become a core technology of the second quantum revolution.
